::: {.callout-note .tldr-tile title="⟡Long story short"}

**Don’t just ask, “How many?” Ask, “How much harm?”** Looking at frequency alongside severity and patient outcomes gives infection-prevention teams a fuller starting point for deciding what to investigate next.

:::

How can a country have a relatively low prevalence of infection among hospital patients, yet a higher estimated burden across its population? It sounds like a mismatch, but the two measures answer different questions.

@zacher2019 estimated the burden of five selected healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) in Germany and compared it with the EU/EEA. Germany's estimated burden was 308.2 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) per 100,000 people, compared with 290.0 in the EU/EEA. DALYs combine years of healthy life lost through illness and premature death, so they capture health impact as well as case numbers.

That doesn't mean that hospital infection rates are unhelpful. It means they're only a part of the big picture. Let's look at what the comparison can tell us, and what it can't.

## Why the measures can differ

Hospital prevalence is a snapshot of how common infections are among hospital patients. It doesn’t show the full estimated impact across the wider population.

A population-level DALY rate looks beyond the patients in hospital and includes the health lost through illness and premature death. The two results aren’t contradictory. They describe different parts of the picture.

## What does the comparison show?

Looking across the whole population gives a different view. The estimated rates for all three measures were higher in Germany than in the EU/EEA. The DALY uncertainty intervals overlap, though, so it’s best to describe this as a higher estimate, not a definite difference.

@tbl-burden compares the estimated burden across Germany and the EU/EEA.

| Estimated burden per 100,000 people | Germany | EU/EEA |
|---|---:|---:|
| HAIs | 592.1 (521.7–665.8) | 467.9 (456.2–480.2) |
| Attributable deaths | 20.1 (13.4–28.2) | 15.3 (10.2–21.2) |
| DALYs | 308.2 (221.2–416.3) | 290.0 (214.9–376.9) |
: Estimated burden of selected HAIs in Germany and the EU/EEA, with 95% uncertainty intervals. {#tbl-burden}

Source: @zacher2019. UI = uncertainty interval.

## Cases and health impact tell different stories

Urinary tract infections (UTIs) accounted for the largest share of estimated cases, about 45%, but 27% of estimated DALYs. Healthcare-associated pneumonia (HAP) and primary bloodstream infections (BSIs) made up about 28% of cases combined, yet 51% of DALYs.

So the infections that occurred most often were not necessarily the ones contributing the most health loss. Looking at severity and premature death alongside case counts helps fill in that picture.

As @fig-infection-shares makes this contrast easier to see. These are approximate shares for selected infection groups, not all HAIs [@zacher2019].

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-infection-shares
#| fig-cap: "Approximate shares of estimated cases and DALYs for selected HAI groups in Germany, 2011–2012."
#| fig-alt: "Grouped horizontal bars compare cases and DALYs. UTIs account for about 45% of cases and 27% of DALYs. Healthcare-associated pneumonia and primary bloodstream infections combined account for about 28% of cases and 51% of DALYs."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-align: center

library(ggplot2)

share_data <- data.frame(
  infection = factor(
    rep(c("UTIs", "HAP + primary BSIs"), each = 2),
    levels = c("HAP + primary BSIs", "UTIs")
  ),
  measure = factor(
    rep(c("Cases", "DALYs"), times = 2),
    levels = c("Cases", "DALYs")
  ),
  share = c(45, 27, 28, 51)
)

dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.72)

ggplot(share_data, aes(x = share, y = infection, fill = measure)) +
  geom_col(position = dodge, width = 0.56) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(share, "%")),
    position = dodge,
    hjust = -0.2,
    size = 4,
    color = "#33231D"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Cases" = "#59652D", "DALYs" = "#4a0018")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 63),
    breaks = seq(0, 60, 10),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
  ) +
  labs(x = "Share of estimates", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFAF2", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFAF2", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#D9C9AB"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#33231D"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(color = "#33231D"),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    legend.text = element_text(color = "#33231D"),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 20, 10, 10)
  )
```

## What hospital teams can take from this

This comparison isn’t a scorecard for any individual hospital, and it doesn’t tell us what today’s infection burden looks like. It *does*, however, suggest a useful question for quality and safety reviews: are the infections we see most often also causing the greatest harm?

Pair current local infection data with information about severity and patient outcomes before deciding where prevention efforts could make the biggest difference.

## A few important caveats

These are estimates for five selected infections, not every healthcare-associated infection. The study used point-prevalence survey data and modelling to estimate the wider burden, so the results depend on the data and assumptions used. They describe 2011 to 2012, not today’s infection burden, and the DALY uncertainty intervals overlap.

Treat the comparison as a way to understand why different measures matter, not as a current benchmark for Germany or for any individual hospital.

## The takeaway

While hospital prevalence still matters, it just doesn’t tell the whole story on its own. Pairing it with infection severity, patient outcomes, and current local data gives teams a more useful picture when deciding where prevention efforts may help most.
